newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD -Investors eye U.S. and German data.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD -Investors eye U.S. and German data.

text.p: International investors will mainly have eyes for U.S. and German economic releases in the week ahead, analysts said on Friday.

In the U.S., the main focus will be the consumer price index (CPI) on Wednesday, and in Germany inflation data and the IFO business sentiment survey, expected Thursday, should steal the limelight, analysts said.
"The three most important German figures are due out next week," said Julian Jessop, chief European economist at Nikko Securities in London.
"At least two will be good for the market and the riskiest will be the IFO," Jessop said.
On Monday, German cost of living figures are forecast to show a rise of 0.4 percent, 1.7 percent up year on year, and M3 figures for the fourth quarter are expected towards the end of the week.

"M3 we think will be inside the Bundesbank target range and the cost of living figures should show inflation falling again," Jessop said. "The IFO survey should give small uptick...but we are not expecting anything there to change market sentiment."
Brian Venables, senior bond analyst at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam, said he believed the IFO survey to be the most reliable indicator in this economic cycle.
"We're looking for it to be up about half point," he said.
The strength of the IFO survey would come from the weakness in the mark and the resulting improved sentiment in the export market, economists said.
Other analysts were focusing on the U.S. following a spate of figures showing a benign inflationary picture and a succesful quarterly refunding.

"The big number is the U.S. CPI number," said Venables. "It looks as if it's potentially going to be very favourable given the sharp correction that we have seen in energy prices over the last few weeks."
Jessop said much of the positive effects for U.S. markets from the soft inflation outlook was already priced in.
Economists said that while the dollar was riding high, they did not expect any change in the currency market outlook unless the idea of Group of Seven (G7) intervention took hold.
Goldman Sachs senior bond analyst Andy Bevan in London said he thought the mix of the European figures would prove the most interesting next week.
"UK retail sales and and CBI monthly trade survey...may raise worries of strength of underlying activity in the economy," he said.

He said French industrial production data due on Friday were expected to improve. These figures, along with the German data, were gaining added importance in the context of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) as countries struggle to meet the convergence criteria.

Italian markets will be on the lookout for any news of a possible mini-budget. Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Friday he could not rule out a "modest" mini-budget and said he would still like to bring forward the full 1998 budget but needed backing from parliament to do so.
Italy also is expected to have consumer price numbers towards the end of the week, which, if they remain low, could help argue for lower interest rates, analysts said.

But analysts said the mood for Italian debt market convergence had swung recently and many were looking for divergence, especially on any tensions over whether Italy will make the grade for the first wave of countries using the euro.
Elsewhere Japan is due to release industrial production numbers on Monday followed by household spending on Tuesday and trade figures on Thursday. Canada has its 1997/98 federal due on Tuesday.
